items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1976-02-04
items.q: Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club

ctx.x: Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive?

Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular, but to actually have, he moved around too fast. See, if he just stayed like, in Chicago, and worked in clubs, they stationary, like you make a reputation in the town, like Fletcher Henderson was in New York, Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club, Fletcher at the Roseland, you heard him on the radio, Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio, Earl Hines in, in the Grand Terrace in Chicago for…

do you think that, do you think that, that Louis Armstrong, was able to, keep his reputation, even though he traveled, or do you think that he built, his reputation in Chicago, and then when he traveled, it was already behind him?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We’d open there with Cab’s band on a New Year’s Eve, and we’d play there for a month

ctx.x: Do you know if he’s living today?

No. I never checked out on him. Last I saw him in Chicago. We played the Sherman Hotel, and he was one of the waiters in the Sherman Hotel. We played there for seven years, seven seasons, seven New Years’ Eves. We’d open there with Cab’s band on a New Year’s Eve, and we’d play there for a month, [? (inaudible)] in Chicago. We’d be broadcasting. Then we went to Milwaukee, and you played there a week. You went to Bay . . . Green Bay Packers. Where that team’s at? Can’t think of the name of the town.
It’s not in Green Bay, Wisconsin?

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He could punch King Kong. If you make him mad, he would go upside your head.

ctx.x: Quite a few, yeah. Called his one-man band. Sheik of Araby and some other.

That is the story of that. But I was there alone. Who . . . anytime you hit that corner or them street corners, ’30 street [130th Street], ’31st, ’32nd, ’33rd on Seventh Avenue, and you come there, they can tell you ain’t from there, because you don’t wear the clothes they’re wearing. You got on them little Southern clothes, them little suits that they have down here, and the wind is blowing Hawkins, cut that corner, “Hawkins,” they say. [Barker whistles.] “Hear that wind, boy, blowing. Cats . . .” You got one of…

little Mickey Mouse coats on. You got to get your lead sheet. That’s what Steele said. No. “You got to get rid of that lead sheet. Got to get a full arrangement, man.” That’s the way Steele talked. My tutor. My mentor. He say, “You got . . . see that little flimsy suit. You catch pneumonia up there with that. You got to get on some long drawers. Get some bull [? (inaudible)].” Say, “Not cotton. You get wool bull [? (inaudible)].” Say, “It’s a difference, because I’m from the South. I’m telling you I know.” That’s…

items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee mentions Cab Calloway in response to the interviewer's statements about others being in Cab's band, but does not claim a direct personal or professional relationship with Cab himself.

ctx.x: And he went with Cab Calloway's band.
He was my idol. He was the one that I followed in Cab's band. Great bass player.
